title: No. 77 — The Appointing Power Continued and Other Powers of the Executive Considered. (Hamilton)
paragraphs: It has been mentioned as one of the advantages to be expected from the cooperation of the Senate in the business of appointments that it would contribute to the stability of the administration. The consent of that body would be necessary to remove as well as to appoint. A change of Chief Magistrate, therefore, would not produce so violent or general a revolution in the officers of the government as might be expected if he were the sole disposer of offices. Where a man in any post had given satisfactory evidence of his fitness, a new President would be restrained from attempting a change in favor of someone more agreeable to him by the apprehension that the disapproval of the Senate might frustrate the attempt and bring some discredit upon himself. Those who can best estimate the value of a steady administration will be most disposed to prize a provision that ties the official existence of public men to the approval or disapproval of that body — which, owing to the greater permanency of its own composition, will in all probability be less subject to inconstancy than any other branch of the government.

On the union of the Senate with the President in the matter of appointments, it has in some cases been suggested that this would give the President an undue influence over the Senate, and in others that it would have the opposite effect — strong proof that neither suggestion is true.

To state the first in its proper form is to refute it. It amounts to this: the President would have an improper influence over the Senate, because the Senate would have the power of restraining him. This is an absurdity in terms. It cannot be doubted that the entire power of appointment would enable him much more effectively to establish a dangerous empire over that body than a mere power of nomination subject to their control.

Let us consider the converse of the proposition: "the Senate would influence the Executive." As I have had occasion to remark in several other instances, the vagueness of the objection forbids a precise answer. In what manner is this influence to be exerted? Concerning what objects? The power of influencing a person, in the sense used here, must imply the power of conferring a benefit on him. How could the Senate confer a benefit on the President by how it used its right of veto over his nominations? If it is said they might sometimes gratify him by acquiescing in a favorite choice, when public motives might dictate different conduct, I answer that the instances in which the President could be personally interested in the result would be too few for him to be materially affected by the Senate's compliance. The POWER that can originate the disposition of honors and emoluments is more likely to attract than to be attracted by the POWER that can merely obstruct their course. If by influencing the President is meant restraining him, this is precisely what was intended. And it has been shown that the restraint would be salutary, and at the same time would not destroy a single advantage to be looked for from the unrestrained agency of that magistrate. The right of nomination would produce all the (good, without the ill.)(E1) (good of the appointing power, and would in great measure avoid its evils.)(E1)

Comparing the plan for appointing officers of the proposed government with that established by the constitution of this state, a decided preference must be given to the former. In that plan the power of nomination is unequivocally vested in the Executive. And since each nomination must be submitted to the judgment of an entire branch of the legislature, the circumstances surrounding an appointment, from the mode of conducting it, would naturally become matters of public knowledge. The public would be at no loss to determine what part each actor played. The blame for a bad nomination would fall on the President alone and absolutely. The censure for rejecting a good one would lie entirely at the door of the Senate, aggravated by the consideration that they had counteracted the good intentions of the Executive. If a bad appointment were made, the Executive for nominating, and the Senate for approving, would share, though in different degrees, in the opprobrium and disgrace.

The opposite of all this characterizes the manner of appointment in this state. The council of appointment consists of three to five persons, of whom the governor is always one. This small body, shut up in a private apartment impenetrable to the public eye, proceeds to execute the trust committed to them. It is known that the governor claims the right of nomination on the strength of some ambiguous expressions in the constitution. But it is not known to what extent, or in what manner, he exercises it, nor on what occasions he is contradicted or opposed. The censure of a bad appointment, owing to the uncertainty of its author and the lack of a determinate target, has neither poignancy nor duration. And while an unbounded field for cabal and intrigue lies open, all idea of responsibility is lost. The most the public can know is that the governor claims the right of nomination; that two out of the inconsiderable number of four men can too often be managed without much difficulty; that if some members of a particular council should happen to be uncomplying, it is frequently possible to get rid of their opposition by setting the times of meeting in a way that makes their attendance inconvenient; and that, for whatever cause, a great number of very improper appointments are made from time to time. Whether a governor of this state uses the ascendancy he must necessarily have in this delicate and important part of the administration to prefer to offices men best qualified for them, or whether he prostitutes that advantage to the advancement of persons whose chief merit is their implicit devotion to his will and the support of a despicable and dangerous system of personal influence, are questions that — unfortunately for the community — can only be subjects of speculation and conjecture.

Every council of appointment, however constituted, will be a conclave in which cabal and intrigue will have full scope. Their number, without an unwarrantable increase of expense, cannot be large enough to prevent easy combination. And since each member will have his friends and connections to provide for, the desire for mutual gratification will breed a scandalous bartering of votes and bargaining for places. The private attachments of one man might easily be satisfied. But to satisfy the private attachments of a dozen or twenty men would result in a monopoly of all the principal posts of government in a few families, and would lead more directly to an aristocracy or oligarchy than any measure that could be contrived. If, to avoid an accumulation of offices, there were to be frequent change in the persons composing the council, this would involve the harms of a mutable administration in their full extent. Such a council would also be more liable to executive influence than the Senate, because they would be fewer in number and would act less immediately under public inspection. Such a council, in short, as a substitute for the plan of the convention, would produce an increase of expense, a multiplication of the evils that spring from favoritism and intrigue in the distribution of public honors, a decrease of stability in the administration of the government, and a diminution of security against undue influence by the Executive. And yet such a council has been warmly contended for as an essential amendment in the proposed Constitution.

I could not properly conclude my observations on the subject of appointments without taking notice of a scheme for which some — though few — advocates have appeared. I mean that of joining the House of Representatives in the power of making them. I shall, however, do little more than mention it, since I cannot imagine it is likely to gain the support of any considerable part of the community. A body so fluctuating and at the same time so numerous can never be deemed fit to exercise that power. Its unfitness will be plain to all when it is remembered that within half a century it may consist of three or four hundred persons. All the advantages of stability — both of the Executive and the Senate — would be defeated by this union, and infinite delays and embarrassments would be caused. The example of most of the states in their local constitutions encourages us to reject the idea.

The only remaining powers of the Executive are: giving information to Congress of the state of the Union; recommending to their consideration such measures as he judges expedient; convening them, or either branch, on extraordinary occasions; adjourning them when they cannot themselves agree on the time of adjournment; receiving ambassadors and other public ministers; faithfully executing the laws; and commissioning all the officers of the United States.

Except for some cavils about the power of convening either house of the legislature and the power of receiving ambassadors, no objection has been made to this class of authorities — nor could they possibly admit of any. It required, indeed, an insatiable appetite for censure to invent exceptions to the parts that have been excepted to. As to the power of convening either house of the legislature, I shall merely remark that for the Senate at least, we can readily see a good reason for it. Since this body shares power with the Executive in the matter of treaties, it might often be necessary to call it together for that purpose when it would be unnecessary and improper to convene the House of Representatives. As to the reception of ambassadors, what I have said in a former paper will provide a sufficient answer.

We have now completed a survey of the structure and powers of the executive department, which, I have tried to show, combines, as far as republican principles will admit, all the requisites for energy. The remaining inquiry is: does it also combine the requisites for safety in a republican sense — a due dependence on the people, a due responsibility? The answer to this question has been anticipated in the investigation of its other features, and is satisfactorily deducible from these circumstances: the election of the President once every four years by persons immediately chosen by the people for that purpose; and his being at all times liable to impeachment, trial, dismissal from office, disqualification from any other office, and to forfeiture of life and estate by subsequent prosecution in the ordinary course of law. But these precautions, great as they are, are not the only ones the plan of the convention has provided for the public security. In the only instances in which abuse of executive authority was materially to be feared, the Chief Magistrate of the United States would, under that plan, be subjected to the control of a branch of the legislative body. What more could be desired by an enlightened and reasonable people?
E1. These two alternate endings of this sentence appear in different editions.
